rv.q: Lungs is a thrilling meeting of head and heart.
Those lucky enough to secure a ticket to Lungs can revel in an acting masterclass from a perfect stage partnership.
Foy and Smith manage the switches of mood and tone with a virtuosity that verges on ostentatious, and there are very few off-moments in pace.
Smith and Foy are always watchable, and ‘Lungs’ is funny throughout.
This is an absorbing evening not because of any large environmental claims but because of the needling but generous dialogue that takes you into the heart of a couple.
Lungs is a case study in how to tackle a major issue.

Both actors cope brilliantly with the technical and tonal challenges, although the scripted-sounded nature of their verbal emissions can irk and the characters are more like talking predicaments than fully rounded personae.
It is hard to imagine a finer outing for it than Matthew Warchus’ gleaming, ideally paced Old Vic production starring Claire Foy and Matt Smith.
The main attraction of this intoxicating evening lies in the accuracy of the depictions.

Nonetheless, these performers were skilled enough to let us sense the discomfort, doubt and resentment beneath the surface of their stoical characters. I am happy to report that Foy and Smith are equally adept at delivering such ambivalence, common to nearly all long and intimate relationships, at high volume and in equally high gear.
Duncan Macmillan's two-hander is a clever, darting thing, and in the hands of Claire Foy and Matt Smith...it is a bit of a wonder.'
Overall, however, an interesting 60 minute play about the minutiae of relationships is hindered by the injection of an extra 30 minutes of dialogue about environmental issues which adds very little.
Despite fine performances from its two stars in a neat, deft production by Matthew Warchus, however, it’s a bland, self-regarding affair that feels decidedly longer than its 80-minute duration.
What could have been a static, cerebral evening turns out to be an exhilarating roller-coaster of a ride, as Foy and Smith demonstrate their undeniable chemistry and considerable acting skills.
Smith and Foy navigate the issue of climate change on Rob Howell (Matilda)’s smart, minimalist stage with the urgency one would expect.

cn.t: Foy and Smith's magnetic chemistry elevates Macmillan's timely but thin two-hander about a couple debating parenthood amid climate anxiety. Critics praise the sharp performances and intelligent writing, though some find the liberal hand-wringing irritating.
